utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination by Mr. Visnjic will continue in a moment; when it does, please bear in mind that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your evidence to speak the truth will continue to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we'll continue looking at documents, and I want to elicit some comments from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness 3D748. Your Honours, I don't -- Ah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the date is the 28th of April, 1999, isn't it, the Supreme Command Staff. This is about the involvement of students from military schools in war units, it's an explanation. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly comment on this. It's related to the evidence you gave yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The VJ in April or in late April was at the apex of its activity facing a very complex situation. It was looking for people to draft in order to be able to carry out its task of defending the country successfully. Among many proposals that cropped up, there was the proposal to draft students of military schools and use them in VJ units. It was the training administration that was in charge of implementing this, and we ourselves, the recruitment, mobilisation, and mobilisation administration or the third administration as we were called presented our own position. We said there was enough military conscripts as it was and it wasn't necessary to draft these students. We said they should continue to be trained and educated and drafted at a later stage when necessary. As you can see, the Chief of the General Staff accepted these positions that we presented and adopted this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the following document, 3D481.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you see that document, right, this is the Supreme Command Staff command for the 14th of April, 1999. This is about volunteers, about taking in volunteers, admitting volunteers, if you like. We've spoken about this already. Just a brief comment, please, if you like.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, this is one in a series of documents aimed at regulating the intake and admission of volunteers into the ranks of the army. I think this is one of the last documents in the series. This is a continuation of an order, I think, an order dated the 7th of April. So if we could please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown what is in actual fact the last page of this document, which I believe is page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. This document shows you the whole system. The admission of volunteers was raised to a new, higher level, new assignments were given, and new men were drafted. The system was enhanced. There's an explanation that goes with this. We later got volunteers involved in the different branches up to 40 years of age. What does it mean when I say the different arms of service or branches, I mean those arms of service that were under the greatest strength and bore the greatest brunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you said something about subordination and resubordination yesterday. What I want to do is show you three documents in relation to this topic and perhaps you can shed some light on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness 3D760. 3D760 -- 670, 670.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you see this document, this is an order of the president, Slobodan Milosevic, dated the 18th of April, 1992 -- 1999.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now on to P1460.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The date is the 18th of April, 1999, by the Supreme Command Staff. Do you see this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, P1457 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move on it may save some time if I indicate that the date on the translation is the 19th of April. I think that should be corrected to the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, P1457.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is an order by the 3rd Army command dated the 20th of April, 1999. General, could you please comment on these three documents you have just been shown, especially in relation to your evidence yesterday about resubordination of the MUP units to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third one has now vanished from the screen, but I think that is the order by the 3rd Army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's P1457. We'll just wait for the B/C/S to come up. You see this, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Comment, please, all three, if you can.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite simple, really, I made two or three references to this yesterday indirect ones but now I'll try to be more specific. When there is armed struggle in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and it is specified who is in charge of the arms struggle and what the other participants do, and this specifically is about the MUP. This means that amid combat operations the organisation in charge is the army. This was clearly defined on the Law on Defence, this 16 and 17. We see that the president emphasised that one should stay; in keeping with this, he forwarded this to the Chief of the General Staff, and in keeping with the prevailing hierarchy to the 3rd Army commander, and these decisions were regulated. In order for the whole system to be harmonized, well harmonized I should say, it was a good thing that they had these three documents that would follow a different chain, chain of communication, it was about cooperation and coordination in keeping with Article 16 and 17, and that was supposed to go through the MUP but it wasn't shown here. One can see here specifically that the VJ units had the responsibility of coordinating and acting in concert with the MUP as soon as combat operations were afoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, based on what you know, what about the implementation of these orders at lower levels, the levels where this coordination was supposed to occur in combat operations? Were there any problems with this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge about combat operations themselves is indirect. I only know what the assistant Chief of the General Staff told us at briefings. I knew about other things that had nothing to do with combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you attended collegium meetings or any other meetings, did you ever hear of a plan, an operation perhaps, anything at all about the expulsion of ethnic Albanians from Kosovo, something that was organized by the VJ or another state institution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm stunned into disbelief -- I was stunned into disbelief to hear this at a later date, actually. Quite the contrary, in fact. Every time I went to these collegium meetings, I was always invited, I was called upon to brief on a number of matters. And every time I was in touch with my superiors as well as my subordinates -- any time I was in touch with anyone in the army, all they ever spoke of was protecting the population and what they had in mind was the population in its entirety. As a person involved with the military obligation issues, I can say that no discrimination ever took place in this respect, and that is precisely why we followed a very cautious system of regulating this military obligation in order not to cause any unnecessary unpleasantness to military conscripts that might have been caused by the Kosovo Liberation Army in the territory of Kosovo for as long as those people were observing their military duty, military responsibilities or responsibilities towards the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm Djuro Cepic. On this morning I represent the Defence of General Lazarevic. I have several questions for you. Yesterday during your evidence you explained about manpower level, how units were replenished with goods and material supplies. What I want to know is where were these goods kept that were supposed to be used as supplies for VJ units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material goods that were to be used as supplies for military units were kept in several different locations and I'll try to explain briefly the essence of this problem. The army's goods are kept in units, they are kept in storage units, warehouses, which may be in barracks or wherever a particular unit is deployed. There are special storage facilities sometimes located in whichever area a unit happens to be in. Material goods, listed material goods, stayed with the owner. As part of its plans, the army on an annual basis reviews these goods to avoid a situation where, for example, there had to be some active involvement on the part of the army and the goods turned out to be not in good working order. So there's an annual review of these, and this is something coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would I be right, General, in saying that pursuant to the rule on mobilisation a military conscript can sign for a uniform, a weapon, and other types of equipment as well and just keep these at home?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're absolutely right, but there's one thing that we must bear in mind. There are huge levels. You have levels that kept everything at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, let me speak briefly about the civil defence and civil protection. Can you tell me how civil defence units are set up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil defence units are set up based on decisions by the defence minister and the assistant minister for civil defence. These are set up based on special orders, they're organized in a particular way, and they have a particular establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The same question in relation to civil protection units, please, so how are these units established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units are established according to the same principle, like the civil defence units, except that their purpose is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell me who commands patrols, guards, and other units of the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system of commanding civil defence and civil protection units is under the Ministry of Defence, and this system of command goes from the minister via the assistant ministers, the centres for defence, to departments for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to look at records of conscripts. General, am I right if I say that in addition to the basic records of conscripts attached to the military territorial organ, there are also records that are kept by civil defence units -- organs and MUP organs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. The basic records are kept in the military territorial command, and everyone that military conscripts are assigned to keep their own records and they have to keep them in line with the basic records.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit Number 5D1183. Your Honour, unfortunately, this document also hasn't got translation, but I will try to ask the witness very, very short question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- Please, [indiscernible] 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please read 5.2, "Changes in Units," just slowly so we have it all in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In order to be brought into the military records of -- in the military department of Kosovska Mitrovica, 136 Albanians were called up, six responded; and in the military district of Pec, five were called up and six responded," in Pec they probably also mean Albanians as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that's an accurate translation, five were called up and six responded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is exactly what is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's accurate translation, Your Honour. Could we scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you recognise the heading of this document? Did you confirm what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document of the 3rd Army dated the 13th of February, 199 -- we cannot see the number of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the course of your testimony yesterday you explained in detail that ethnic Albanians from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were brought into military records in 1999 as well. Does this document confirm that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be the right moment for me to make a comment with regard to what the honourable Judge noticed; namely, that five were called up and six responded. By your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I assume one brought a friend along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Viewed this way, it looks illogical; however, practice is different. When you call-up one military conscript and when he says where he's going to, as is the case of records, then it often happens that another military conscript comes along to be recorded in the records. So this information is correct and a frequent occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, was the functioning of the Army of Yugoslavia analysed from the point of view of humanitarian law in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within each annual analysis of combat-readiness and the functioning of the army, this is carried out regularly. As for 1998, it is characteristic from yet another aspect. The International Red Cross, according to its own plan, visited all the arms and services of the Army of Yugoslavia and viewed combat documents that are prepared for an issue to the army, the combat rules that define training, and it viewed how training actually takes place in the Army of Yugoslavia. During the final analysis in November of 1998 where I was in attendance, too, as a representative of the General Staff of the army, the representatives of the International Red Cross that were highly represented, I don't remember the exact name of their representative, Thompson I think it was, then there was retired Australian general, then there was another retired general from Switzerland and yet another member was frigate captain from the US navy. It was established that all international and humanitarian laws were incorporated into the rules of the Army of Yugoslavia and were abided by in the Army of Yugoslavia. In a way, they expressed their conviction that they will be further promoted and be an example to the surrounding area. I think that this was a major success on the part of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, there must be a report of this visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will try to do my best to find that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the sort of thing you would expect if you're going to rely on this that you would produce the material from the horse's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, for many years you dealt with the organization of the army. In this courtroom the name of a Joint Command has often been referred to. Could you please explain for us what "command" means as a concept.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organization is my basic line of work. That is what I worked on. As for the word itself, "command," if you're referring to an organizational unit, it constitutes the name of an organizational unit that is used by different organs and different organizations and represents the managerial part of an organization.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is necessary, what elements are required for a command to be able to function? What does it consist of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for a command to make sense and to be able to exist and function aless its sense is its very self which would make it nonsensical, it has to have a clearly defined managerial component, it has to have clearly defined rights, it has to have clearly defined obligations, it has to have clearly defined proponents, and it has to have clearly defined who is at the top of this command; and then the next part: Clearly defined units and organs which it commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What kind of reporting structure must exist in that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every command, every command and all actions that start has to work the other way around. This feedback is regulated in a particular way, but at any rate there are different types of reporting depending on the numbers involved in military institutions above battalion level it is compulsory to have reporting in writing. And that is subdivided into regular reports and extraordinary reports or special reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So incoming and outgoing reports have to be in writing, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about organization, do you know that for the functioning of a command at operational level, in this specific case a corps, what is the number of optimal links between the command and the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rule of organization that you were asking me about is not representative only for a corps. It is a general rule in organization. In order to have successful command a superior who commands should have at an optimum six to eight links with those below him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that the Pristina Corps in the war had 26 links, according to the chain of command, organizational and resubordinated units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I'm not sure it's 26, maybe it's even more, and it has to do with a particular practice that was quite represented in organization until I came; namely, that the number of links went up without distribution of these links according to internal organs. Later on we worked on the reduction of these links, or rather, the optimisation of command. However, up until the period that we're talking about now, we did not achieve any major results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you should know that I don't understand this, what the six to 8 links are about and what the 26 are about. So it would be helpful if you were to explore this a little further.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, am I right that these links constitute links between the command, in this particular case the Pristina Corps, and the subordinated units, brigades and others?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, and that can be explained easily in relation to the observation of His Honour, that this is the number of units that is directly subordinated of the commander of the operative entity. In this case, the number of units directly subordinated to the commander of the Pristina Corps, that is to say 26 units were directly subordinated to the commander of the Pristina Corps and at every point in time he had to have contact with each and every one of those commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I think I understand that, but the original answer from the witness was: "This rule of organization that you were asking me about is not representative only for a corps. It is a general rule in organization. In order to have successful command, a superior who commands should have at an optimum six to eight links with those below him." Now, that suggests to me if you've got 26 there's something wrong, if the optimum is six to eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, was it allowed to have such a big number of links?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretical recommendations are one thing, or rather, the optimum required, and what is actually assigned is a different matter. The question and answer precisely relies on that, that at this point in time there was an organization with a larger number of links than allowed for by theory. That was practice until then and that practice was supposed to be changed, but it was being changed slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question to complete my understanding of this. Does that mean at the lowest level, in a platoon, the commander would have -- in an ideal platoon the commander would have six to eight men under him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There aren't any men in a platoon, there are squads. It says six to eight links, so a platoon commander has three, a commander of a company has, or rather, three to six companies, and then if you were to go up to a higher level this unit number were to go up. You would see in the Pristina Corps there was a total of 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I would just interrupt to request the honourable counsel if he could provide us with a little chart showing how this pyramid is formed between links and highest echelons, that will make it very, very easy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to say it, it is quite difficult right now, but in short time of period, I will prepare --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: At your convenience, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The picture is much clearer now, Mr. Cepic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question in relation to this, General. Does that mean that functioning was seriously impeded because of this large number of links?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This functioning was impeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we've mentioned the Pristina Corps, do you know who was at its head during the aggression on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do, it was another one of my classmates from school, General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us a bit more about General Lazarevic, what kind of a person he is and what kind of a soldier he is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for General Lazarevic, his assessments speak in itself and his results. I would just like to say a few basic things, in view of the brevity of time. He is a high professional, responsible, hard-working, industrious, and above all a humane person. I would like to give you an example. He is the last person who left the territory of Kosovo only after all his soldiers had left, when he saw that all of his soldiers had left, it is only then that he himself left the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: General, I have little explanation for myself, I beg of that. When you say with so many links within the organization there were impediments and there were difficulties and this impeded the progress, do you mean to say there was inherent organizational defects in the system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you said inherent. There were inherent, in-built problems, if you like that a commander had to deal with. There were certain ways of dealing with these problems. He resubordinate some of the units to his logistics assistant, some to the Chief of Staff, and some to perhaps another officer, and the goal that he keep in mind while doing this was to keep intact the singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General, my name is Dan Ivetic and I am the attorney for Sreten Lukic. I will have some questions for you today regarding the testimony you gave over the last two days. Now, first of all, you testified that they MUP and VJ were two different systems and "not a single unit of the MUP was part of the establishment of the VJ for that matter to find in theory," transcript 81, lines 6 through 7. I would like you to follow of up on that and I would like to ask you if any single organ or unit of the VJ was ever part of the establishment of the MUP or subordinate to any MUP organ even in theory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to begin with. It's difficult for me to speak about how the MUP was organized. I never saw their charts or diagrams, but I don't think that would be a possibility because of the discrepancies between the two systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But my question was relating to organs of the VJ. Apparently you are quite familiar with all the organs of the VJ. Wouldn't you agree with me that it would be impossible for any organ of the VJ ever to become subordinate to any organ of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, no not in any sense that the army unit could never be subordinated to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like a more specific question, if possible. I think I know what you are alluding to, but in order for me to be able to provide a more specific answer perhaps I could use a more specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon your knowledge of the functioning and operations of the VJ and the applicable laws in effect, could you ever foresee a situation when an organ of the VJ were to be part of the establishment of the MUP or subordinated to a MUP organ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter, yes, and this was known to happen in practice. A subordinate officer carried out tasks within, there was coordination, but he was never part of the MUP because MUP had no bodies that were able to run a system like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic has shown you Exhibit 3D670, the order of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia dated 18 April 1999 in which it specifically states that pursuant to Article 17 of the Law on Defence units and organs of the interior on the territory of Yugoslavia are to be resubordinated to the Yugoslav Army officer planning, organizing, and commanding combat operations according to the tasks received in the assigned zones of responsibility. Have you ever seen any other order from the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia specifically resubordinating the MUP of Serbia exclusively to the Pristina Corps, as at least one other witness has indicated here today -- excuse me, has indicated here in this trial?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but in order to explain this order and in order to understand its essence, one must read carefully Article 16 and a 17 of the Law on Defence because this order is a continuation of just that and what is specified there. It's what the exact moment is, when this is done, and how this resubordination is done. Therefore, this order without Article 17, which is what the president document specifies, has an entirely different meaning. If you read carefully Article 17 of the Law on Defence and the meaning suddenly becomes very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm pausing to wait for the translation and the transcript to catch up with us. And am I correct that Article 17 specifically states that organs of the MUP may be resubordinated to the army commander only in the course of combat operations that are underway, combat actions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that pursuant to resubordination under Article 17 of the Law on Defence, the peacetime role of the MUP is not to be affected by the implementation of a resubordination order; that is to say, the VJ does not control the peacetime or regular activities of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't speak of their control in peacetime or wartime activities because the purpose and the tasks of the MUP are different from those of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could return to 3D670, and that is the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That last answer, Mr. Ivetic, doesn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, Article 17 of the Law on Defence on resubordination does not affect the regular functioning and duties of MUP Secretariats of the Interior, police stations, or OUPs, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Article 17 of the Law on Defence only applies to actual individual combat operations once they are ordered or undertaken; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When undertaken, then there is cooperation or concerted action, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can return to 3D670 for a moment, that's the order dated April 18th, 1999, from the federal president of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, at the time. I presume, sir, that you don't have any personal knowledge as to whether this particular order issued by the president of the FRY was ever forwarded to the minister of the interior, Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic of the Serbian MUP, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could focus -- I believe we have the order on the screen. It would appear, focusing on the second and third paragraphs of the order, that the chief of the Supreme Command Staff is tasked with forwarding an appropriate order to civilian organs and taking necessary steps to effectuate that order. Now, we've had one witness, General Simic, that testified that no such steps were taken by the Supreme Command Staff to send anything to Minister Stojiljkovic of the MUP and indeed P1460, which Mr. Visnjic showed you likewise as not having it being addressed to the MUP. Do you, sir, know if any such written communication or order or written document was ever sent by the Supreme Command Staff or the command of the 3rd Army to Minister Stojiljkovic or anyone in the MUP hierarchy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at item 3 of the order that I have in front of me it reads: "Chief of the Supreme Command Staff will send his requests to the civilian government organs and other defence bodies," his requests, not his orders. Requests. Now, how are these passed along? This goes down the chain of command to the next link, as it were, and requests are made at this borderline where cooperation takes place with the MUP. So he forwards this order to the army commander, he in turn to the corps commander, and then it was at the level of brigades and battalions that requests were eventually submitted and that concerted action was agreed upon with the other units, and that was the only thing that was possible at the time. As for cooperation with any other civilian bodies, the request only implies what is strictly necessary for the coordination to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Any requests to the MUP would have occurred at the lower level where any combat operations were undertaken; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're touching on something that is best viewed in its entirety and not just bit by bit. The powers of the MUP and the powers of the VJ are very different. The army is the a federal institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Functioning of the MUP which you already said you don't have knowledge of, then we'll be spinning our wheels needlessly. One moment.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't headed that way, truth to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me take a step back and try and frame it in terms of testimony you've already given. In your direct examination you stated that the same three commands, going from the highest level down to the lowest level, ought to be within the parallel system of the MUP. How is that to be effectuated if the top of the MUP was not to be advised of the resubordination order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I was shown those three documents, or rather, orders by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Chief of the General Staff, and the 3rd Army commander, I commented at the time by saying that this system had to be harmonized and this had to be implemented and one should look at orders that were sent along the chain of command to the MUP. I said then that I had never seen those orders, but what I did see is a clear definition for these requests to be agreed upon at appropriate levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know, I'll move on. Sir, do you have personal knowledge of any written decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That last sentence, what did you mean by what you did see is a clear definition for these requests to be agreed upon at appropriate levels? Where did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order that was submitted by the president to the Chief of the General Staff, the Chief of the General Staff to the 3rd Army commander, and he implements this and this ensures that there is cooperation and coordination at the level at which combat operations take place and combat operations takes place -- combat operations take place at levels between the brigade and the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What Mr. Ivetic is suggesting is rather strange, is that this would not be communicated to the top level in the MUP so that they could make sure there were no misunderstandings further down the line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you have personal knowledge of any written decision or communication sent by Minister of the Interior Stojiljkovic or any other senior MUP official to the VJ, that is, to the Supreme Command Staff or even any of the army commands, refusing to implement any valid resubordination request?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing to indicate that. I think those might have been requests for concerted action or coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that -- strike that. Have you ever read of any reported problems arising from specific MUP units refusing to obey combat orders or instructions from any army commander at the brigade level relative to combat actions through the reading of any combat reports, "borbeni izvestaj," read or received by you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have knowledge about other areas, but not about combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that you have previously testified that resubordination only applies to combat actions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite precise, resubordination and coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll take that as a yes. Now -- thank you. When you say that you had knowledge about other areas, was that knowledge ever reported in any form to Minister Stojiljkovic of the MUP to apprise him of the same?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about other areas, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was happening for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When, in fact, was the first time that you personally heard of any major problems from resubordination and was this in 2001?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2001, I was working in an entirely different area in 2001 and it has nothing to do with this. This was about KZB.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday at transcript page 81, lines 17 through 18, you seemed to indicate that there was some degree of confusion regarding interpretation of what was actually implied under Article 17 and resubordination. Would you agree with me that expecting the minister of the interior to be directly resubordinated to the General Staff or to the staff of the Supreme Command and sitting in the command centre of the VJ is not a proper understanding of resubordination according to Article 17 of the Law on Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been part of the system for a very long time. There was no such request by the army ever. I don't believe the army would ever have made such a request for the minister of the interior to go to the General Staff, sit there and do something for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, sir; however, we did have several VJ officers come here and testify that precisely this was their understanding of resubordination, including Colonel Pesic who testified for the Prosecution. Now, likewise, if someone were to proclaim that the VJ were in charge of customs and that the assistant ministers of the RJB and RDB of the MUP as well as the chiefs of the secretariats were to sit at the command of either the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd Armies and be directly resubordinated to the commander of those armies, that, too, would not be a proper implementation or interpretation of Article 17 of the Law on Defence, would it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that Colonel Pesic is not competent to comment on that. For a while he was my subordinate, for a while I was professionally above him. I don't think that he knows that area. As for his subjective comments, that is his own affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thank you for that. Now, could you actually answer the other part of the question, that is to say: If someone were to proclaim that the VJ were in charge of customs and that the assistant ministers of the RJB and RDB of the MUP as well as the chiefs of the secretariats of the MUP were to sit at the commands of either the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd Armies and be directly resubordinated to the commander of those armies, that, too, would not be a proper implementation or interpretation of Article 17 of the Law on Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is impossible. The army can never be in charge of customs or does it have such organs, so the example is quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about the part of the assistant chiefs of the RJB and the RDB sitting at the command -- at the army level and being subordinated to the commander along with the "nacelniks" or the chiefs of the SUPs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what direction this is moving in. I was very clear when I talked about subordination and coordination of combat activities in accordance with Articles 16 and 17. Everything beyond that is something quite different or even constitutes theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question's quite specific, though, from your knowledge of the way in which things were done in the army you're being asked to say whether it's conceivable that the assistant chiefs of the RJB and RDB could be sitting in a command post along with senior army officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm actually asking whether it's conceivable under Article 17 specifically, whether that article foresees such an occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that question presupposes that there is combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible for them to be sitting there and exchanging views, but this is not sitting and exchanging views, but it is not coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the transcript says: "But it is not coordination," the witness I believe said it was not resubordination. I don't know how that came through on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, am I correct that insofar as a state of war had not previously been declared in the FRY and that Article 17 had not previously been invoked, that there was a fair degree of confusion and uncertainty among many within the VJ, I'll limit it to that because you stated your knowledge was limited to the VJ, there was uncertainty by many of what exactly was meant by Article 17 and resubordination, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few problems and quite a bit of confusion. Yesterday I said very precisely that Article 17 constitutes a good solution; however, I did not say that it is a well-regulated system because for Article 17 to be a good system there would have to be a well-regulated system of armed forces, defence, security sector, and then there would be no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you to comment upon two situations in the field during the course of the war in Kosovo-Metohija. First of all, I'd like to ask you if you're familiar - and I'll I'm asking you we can put up 6D117, which is the document which forms the basis for my question - are you familiar or aware, sir, with an order written by the command of the 69th military territorial detachment at Istok to form a staff under the command of Captain Princip Milosavljevic, who was the commander of that detachment to place all governmental and municipal organs on the territory of Istok municipality under his command for the functioning of life and work in the zone of responsibility of Istok. Are you familiar with this order that's on the screen, although for some reason we don't have the translation which I do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the other document that we had, actually. I don't know what this one is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure that this is the document that General Lukic's Defence was looking for. I'm trying to see whether it's on their list, on their announced list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of this morning it is. [In English] I was just trying to be fair to the witness. I could ask the witness the question without the use of the document since I was just asking him if he was aware of any situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We weren't aware of the document on the list when the witness testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just take it away, Mr. Ivetic, ask your question without it let's get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any order of the 69th military detachment stating that all republican and municipal government organs on the territory of Istok municipality are hereby placed under the command of the 69th VTOD Istok? I believe I said republican and municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for such an order, I heard about it after the war when the work of territorial commands was being analysed, and my comment was, Does this person still work for the military or has he been kicked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I had to wait again for the transcript. I take it again, sir, that you do not agree that his actions were appropriate under the law?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Inter alia I think I said yesterday that the Army of Yugoslavia is one of the rare military organizations that does not have organs for establishing civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to complete the circle, are you aware of any similar undertaking or order by the command of the Pec Vojni Odsek whereby Lieutenant-Colonel Dusko Antic attempts to order all federal and republican authorities on the territories of the municipality of Pec, Istok, Klina and Decani to be under the command of the Pec Vojni Odsek or military territorial organ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something about this; however, what I heard is insufficient, I believe, for me to be able to provide competent testimony at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I sincerely thank you for your time and your answers. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: May I beg of you a minute, please. Now, General, kindly refer to your previous answer that you gave that you may have heard something about this formation under Lieutenant-Colonel Dusko and Pec Vojni Odsek you may have heard about it, but you don't have sufficient knowledge about it or information, but tell me can such a thing happen at that level without the higher echelons knowing about it or without their permission, can that happen within that organization unless there were provisions like Article 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the situation as it was at that point in time in Kosovo and Metohija, in view of the problems that were there sometimes people even with the best of intentions go beyond their rights and powers. I did not hear of this because I was not the superior of that military department, but I was the professional organ and I'm convinced that the command reacted quickly as soon as they heard about that because this impedes the further functioning of the military and if you wish it even imposes certain obligations on the military that it can never carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that a battalion commander may take goods for replenishment of his unit and issue a certificate for the goods that he has taken. Are you speaking about the commandeering of articles from the civilian population or from individuals who are not members of the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commandeering is probably some kind of a legal term. I am talking about how it was defined according to the law; that is to say, supplying the army with military resources, taking goods from replenishment, that is to say from private individuals, state organs, socially owned organizations and enterprises, and so on there is a clearly defined legal procedure that is applied. However, at the point in time when centres for defence for the Ministry of Defence do not function and when the Ministry of Defence cannot according to plan replenish a unit with certain goods only in special extraordinary situations, the commander of the battalion can replenish his unit with available resources and issue a certificate stating that this resource had been taken. What -- how you put this in legal terms, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I withdraw the word "commandeer." He can take goods or articles from members of the civilian population without their consent if it is needed for the army and give them a certificate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The goods, among other things, would include -- could include motor vehicles that might be needed for military operations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he has to have grounds for that. Now, what are grounds for something like that? Grounds for something like that is that he is entitled to a motor vehicle, that he does not have a motor vehicle, that the system is not functioning, and thereby conditions are created for him to take that motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, he issues to the citizen or the person from who it is taken a certificate. Does he retain a copy of that certificate or a document showing the circumstances under which this article, this motor vehicle, had been taken?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact format of this certificate is in all mobilisation plans of all units and institutions. You can get a copy and you can have a look at it. I cannot remember every one of the entries now, but I know that it is exactly prescribed what it's supposed to look like. This is contained in mobilisation plans, and then commanders, when necessary, use these certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And he should retain a certificate, a copy of the certificate, or some record of what has been taken and from whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things it is that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Therefore, in respect to all articles seized by the military in Kosovo during the conflict in 1999, particularly the motor vehicles, there should be a record of who these motor vehicles belong to and the circumstances under which they were taken?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used a term in relation to all articles. That is not precise. I said that it was planned, exactly envisaged, there are certain records of these articles, exactly when this was looked at or was taken from, and so on. So it takes place according to that plan. This just has to do with part of the articles that are commander of battalion, division, and further up can take in a situation when the Ministry of Defence does not function in that particular territory. If that system functions, then the order is quite different. It is as I explained it initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: However, there should be a record, an inventory, of all the articles, including motor vehicles, that were seized by members of the army from civilians in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there should be a record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where would this record be kept -- well, I assume that the battalion commander at the lowest level would have the authority to do these seizures. He would at least start the process of record-keeping. Would the -- would he have an obligation to submit those records to higher command offices?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on Defence and the decrees regulating this subject matter refer to taking not seizing, so these are two different concepts. You keep referring to seizures, and that is quite different, basically different inter alia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, please. You know perfectly well what is being talked about here. Now, Mr. Stamp, the beginning of that question was fine. Why did you get into the complicated bit? All you would need to say is: Where would this record be kept, and we can make progress from there. So you've already told us, Mr. Kosovac, there would be a record particularly including if motor vehicles are taken, where would that record be kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The records of motor vehicles do exist and they're in the territorial organ and in the civil defence organ. The records on motor vehicles taken under extraordinary circumstances are established later once the battalion commander informs his superior command of a situation that occurred, but that is a special situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would records of vehicles in the possession of the military - and I'm speaking specifically of the Pristina Corps - be kept at the Pristina Corps headquarters or at the 3rd Army headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps headquarters that is guarded with -- that is kept with the mobilisation plans; at the level of the army, there are surveys, summary surveys, not records.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move on and discuss a little bit the issue of mobilisation. You said there were some 6.000 volunteers mobilised during the conflict. Is -- am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 6.000 volunteers that had volunteered, that had volunteered in the army during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Well, let me get straight to the point. Do you know how many volunteers were sent to units that were subordinated to the Pristina Corps in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I did have those surveys in my own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate in any way now, but I can provide a copy of these surveys because I know where they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, we would like you to help us. You know that there was 6.000 who volunteered. Roughly how many of them were subordinate -- were in units subordinated to the Pristina Corps in Kosovo? We won't hold it against you if it's not entirely accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for that. But you know what the problem is? The problem is that the volunteers went to units that were later resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. So if I were to come up with something now -- well, it must have been over 70 per cent for the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps, rather. But then we are counting to -- counting on many other units that were resubordinated to them, like the 252nd, 37th, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you were aware that volunteers being conscripted or being accepted into the army might be problematic. This was an awareness that you in the General Staff had even before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was part of the General Staff, so if I was aware of that, the General Staff was aware of that. Before the conflict broke out, we did not have any volunteers, we did not register any. Perhaps you heard that according to law people could ask to do their military service earlier, but these were not volunteers. This is simply a request to do your military service earlier. The term "volunteer" only has to do with war and mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to understand it was known that volunteers presented certain problems. And in the context of Kosovo and Metohija where there had been over a long period of time conflict, ethnic conflict, and animosity arising therefrom, it was known by the persons in the command of the VJ that volunteers in Kosovo would present even greater possibilities for problems for indiscipline and abuse.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw that the first order about volunteer was issued on the 24th of March. Yugoslavia was attacked on the 23rd of March; that is to say that we in the General Staff immediately assumed that once people started volunteering there would be a problem. Our assumption was correct. We were not afraid of volunteers in terms of the interethnic conflict because the units were stable, composed, homogenous. We were afraid of volunteers who were criminals, and our overall activity was geared towards preventing at a maximum level for having someone like that enter the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: However, in the context of Kosovo, which is what I'm asking about, and the history of ethnic conflict there was a danger not only from persons who were criminals but from persons who volunteered to go to Kosovo because they may have had scores to settle on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Settling scores on an individual basis with anyone along ethnic lines is crime, but you couldn't have such a person taking along an entire unit for a settling of scores along ethnic lines. This didn't happen. Why did someone loot someone else? Why did someone kill someone else? Was it hatred? Was it ethnic hatred? I think that's a different kettle of fish altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if that is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Kosovac, we have to break at this stage for 20 minutes. Could you please leave the court with the usher and we'll see you again at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that there were approximately 150 foreign volunteers who were persons from the Republika Srpska or from Croatia considered to be foreign volunteers.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what I said about 150 foreign volunteers, I didn't mention where they were from. I did say later that about 10.000 volunteers had put in a request from other countries, but the answer is no. These were volunteers from all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If someone, a Serb, from Croatia or from Republika Srpska applied to be a volunteer, would he be considered foreign volunteer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever is not a citizen of Yugoslavia is a foreigner, regardless of the fact that this person may, in fact, be an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you have any criteria for the reception of volunteers? Did they have to conform to any particular standards to be considered to be volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the orders that were shown yesterday - and I think one was even shown today - it is clear that there were a set of firm criteria that were set which we now to have forgotten about. Number one, a volunteer is a military conscript, which means that this volunteer has a military record, so to speak, that he is trained, and that he is fit to fight as a volunteer. Another criterion was that this person was never assigned to a different unit. Accepting this person as a volunteer would mean depriving that other unit of one of its members. The third thing was being medically fit and this was subject to certain medical checks. The fourth criterion was among other things that a candidate has been vetted by appropriate security bodies. There were other criteria, too. So, for example, a volunteer could be up to 40 years of age. That was in the various arms of service. As for all the technical sectors, quartermasters, and such-like, those persons qualified as long as they were under 60 years of age. So these criteria were really quite clear-cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So in terms of accepting a volunteer, the volunteer would have had to provide proof that he or she was militarily trained?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as you establish that a person is in possession of a military record, this proves that this person at some point underwent military training and you also know exactly what kind of training the person did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were aware, were you, that paramilitaries posed another set of problems, that paramilitaries were involved in and responsible for many crimes that were committed in Kosovo. Were you aware of that at the beginning of the conflict or during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a generally known fact to whoever knew something about this that there were paramilitary formations emerging in the territory of the SFRY, but there were other bodies that were in charge of these paramilitary units. Bearing that in mind, when we organized for these volunteers to be admitted, we did this on an individual basis, in a bid on our part to prevent the formation of any paramilitary organizations. In military and territorial commands, volunteers were admitted on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well -- excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You refer there to the SFRY. We're talking here in -- about 1999 and the problem of paramilitaries at that time. Now, what was the position then? What was your knowledge of the activities of paramilitaries in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned the SFRY as an area not as a country. I'm talking about the area throughout which there existed paramilitary formations. They were all over the place and they were moving about hither and tither, but that was not what I meant to observe. The gist is we admitted volunteers on an individual basis in a bid to prevent the formation of any paramilitary entities to the extent that we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I was asking you is: What did you know, if anything, about the involvement of paramilitaries in crimes in Kosovo in 1999? Did you have reports of their involvement in crimes in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of those reports because those reports were reaching the legal administration, and this was in the same sector that I worked in. I heard about crimes that occurred, I heard about people who were brought to justice, and I heard about those that no charges were pressed against, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I proceed can I just ask you about an answer you gave earlier. You said that there were paramilitary formations emerging in the territory of the SFRY. Well, there were other bodies that were in charge of these paramilitary units. What were the bodies that were in charge of these paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a paramilitary unit was moving about a certain area that was probably under the jurisdiction of the MUP in terms of a paramilitary unit joining the army, in terms of preventing this, I mean, that would be the army. But, for example, if a paramilitary unit tried to move from one area to the other I think the border patrols would have the responsibility of stopping them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one correction in transcript, page 39, line 12, I think that the witness also said [Interpretation] "There were arrests." [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when you say that there were persons or bodies that were in charge of the paramilitaries, you are speaking about the MUP and border units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about everyone, everyone had their own responsibilities. All I did was name an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, could you name -- well, first tell me what do you mean when you say that there were bodies in charge of the paramilitaries? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is a result of the FRY constitution. Under the constitution, all paramilitary organizations were banned; therefore, jurisdiction over paramilitary organizations, what this means is the power and responsibility to prevent their existence and prevent any support for such paramilitary entities. When I say jurisdiction or in charge or responsibility, that's what I mean, prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said that you are aware that many persons, members of these paramilitaries involved in crimes were not charged --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that misstates the evidence. If he's going to cite to the witness's testimony, I would respect that counsel actually cite the testimony. We've been at this time and again where he mis-cites portions of exhibits and mis-cites testimony of witnesses. Use exact words if we're going to ask the witness to verify his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question to the witness about what he said and I have recorded the gist of the testimony of the witness, but the witness is in a position to say whether or not this is his evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evidence was that he had heard about crimes committed by paramilitaries, there had been some arrests, and others where there were no proceedings. So on that basis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You recall the question. You are aware that many of the paramilitaries -- or there were no proceedings against many of the paramilitaries alleged to be involved in crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never put it like that, nor can I claim to know that. I heard, that doesn't mean I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- And there is an enormous difference between the two. I know that the legal administration, and they were in charge of the judiciary, took measures in coordination with other bodies for everyone to be brought to justice under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were paramilitaries or former members of paramilitary units accepted into the VJ as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military conscripts were admitted as volunteers in cases where nothing stood in the way of this person's admission into the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but didn't you make provisions and didn't you admit into the VJ persons that you knew to be paramilitaries or to have been paramilitaries in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite precise in my answer. In order for someone to be admitted, this person had to meet certain conditions. I told you about the criteria or conditions. No criminal form, plus a number of other conditions that any military conscript must meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're still not answering the -- Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness said that he didn't commit to that -- this person didn't commit any crime, and that is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The question was quite precise, Mr. Kosovac, and you have not answered it in a straightforward way. The question is: Did you ever accept people who had been -- to have been paramilitaries as volunteers? Now, we assume that if you accept them they satisfy the criteria, but were there people who you know had been paramilitaries who satisfied these criteria and were accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military conscripts were admitted as volunteers by military districts, and this is several steps -- several runs in the ladder down from me and I know what the criteria were. Did any of them, for example, know in relation to a specific individual that they had been members of a paramilitary unit? Did they know that this person had no criminal record so they just admitted them? But that was not the criterion for their admission or non-admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it then from your answer that it was within the framework for accepting volunteers into the VJ that a person who had been a paramilitary in Kosovo could be accepted if he completed the procedures that were in place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look quickly at 3D481. This is one of the Supreme Command orders regulating mobilisation on the 14th of April, 1999. If we look at page 2 of the English copy and it's also page 2 of the B/C/S copy, the top of page 2 of the B/C/S copy. You see the second paragraph of section 2.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that provisions were made, specifically made, for the induction of volunteers who had been paramilitaries as long as they completed their procedures that were put in place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me that the Chief of Staff made provisions for the induction of persons who had been volunteers, who had been paramilitaries into the VJ as volunteers so long as they had complied with the procedures that he put in place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2.2 envisages a very clear procedure. I don't see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it's not a problem. I just want to know if you agree with me that the second paragraph of item 2.1 indicates that specific provisions were made for the induction of persons who had been paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you -- with your leave I think it would be fair to show to witness the whole paragraph 1. -- 2.1, because as we see on the screens we just see the last paragraph of that article. So if we can move on on the first page, later on to second, in B/C/S, I've been speaking about B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what you're saying, but that's, in my opinion, unnecessary. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paramilitaries were persons, you said, who had had military training before. When persons were inducted as paramilitaries, what additional training was involved before they were sent off to units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never said anything about the conditions that related to paramilitaries. There must be some criteria and I don't believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I accept that. Volunteers. I'm speaking of volunteers, what additional training did they receive before they were sent off to the units of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think another witness will answer this question for you just fine, it's a witness who is due to appear and he was in charge of training. In the first paragraph on page 2 it says, I forbid that any members of paramilitary units should be admitted as volunteers, and that is perfectly clear, that's one thing. And then you asked me about the possibility of a former paramilitary applying to become a volunteer. Now, these are two entirely different matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now we get exactly to what Mr. Cepic has requested that the witness be shown. Page 44, line 24, in the first paragraph, in the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you'll be able to deal with this in re-examination. You'll get your chance. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you about training. You said that you are not qualified to speak about training or that there are persons better qualified to speak about training of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were other people who were in charge of training volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on from there. You have said on many occasions, even when not asked, that persons were received as volunteers, as individuals and not in units.
