There is a line of questioning I would like to ask about that, but you have also said on two occasions that you know about operations, combat operations, indirectly. So let me ask this first: Would you be able to comment from your knowledge on the use of volunteer units in combat operations in Kosovo by the VJ? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I would not agree with the first statement being made here, that on many occasions I talked about persons being admitted as volunteers even when not asked. If I may remind you yesterday while I was giving evidence the word "units" came up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please just deal with the question that's been asked of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm focusing here on a misstatement. As a result, could you please repeat the entire question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not a misstatement to say that you have on a number of occasions said that volunteers were accepted as individuals and not in units; we're all agreed on that. Let's move on to the question itself. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is inaccurate when counsel stated that I wasn't asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, the question is this: Are you in a position to comment on whether or not volunteer units were used for combat activities in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Phantom unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Phantom, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on. Military territorial units in Kosovo came under the command of the -- of the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at P2930, please, a combat report dated the 31st of March. And if we could move on to the second page in English which is the first page in B/C/S, which is on the screen now, so if we could move to the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Under item 4 it speaks of MUP and military territorial units that are controlling the territory and channelling Siptar refugees to Albania and it's incident free. When two units of this nature are engaged in that type of activity, under whose command are they? Under which -- under the command of which organization are they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two units do not carry out the same control of the territory. Each one of them is within its own organization. When they meet, then they coordinate their activities. The military territorial unit provides security for important facilities in the territory where it is that are of relevance to defence and the military. Entry/exit, barracks, roads leading to warehouses, the areas where the units are deployed, the MUP carries out its own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So in channelling refugees to Albania, they are operating within their own chains of command but in a coordinated manner, as an example of coordination that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. As for channelling, I couldn't say anything. As for channelling, I couldn't say anything specific. I was talking about their authority in terms of controlling the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how do you understand then this statement, that MUP and military territorial units are controlling the territory and channelling the Albanian refugees to the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be immodest if I were not to say that this was not written in an illiterate manner. If I were the superior officer, I would ask for clarification of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It -- very well. The statement, sir, seems -- well, it's very clear on the face of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, it's really for us to decide whether that statement is consistent with other evidence we've heard in the case and might support the case that there was a joint operation to do this. This witness is saying he's got no knowledge of the particular circumstances, and it sounded to me as though you were proceeding to present argument rather than take evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, I think I could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the course of the conflict in 1999 and in the months immediately preceding the conflict, did you become aware of an organ known as the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of the war against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in some talks I did hear mention of some Joint Command; however, since I knew that it was not organized at all in accordance with the rules of organization and that it was not within the organization of the army, I did not particularly ask and I was not consulted either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "in some talks," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you work in the General Staff during the course of a war, you hear different information and different talks. You hear stories, you hear many things that people say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you had regular briefings with other members of the General Staff. Did you hear of the Joint Command in any of these briefings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of the war, I had regular meetings at the collegium of the assistant Chief of General Staff for replenishment, mobilisation, and system-related affairs. These meetings took place at least twice a day. Not a single time did we discuss a Joint Command. Therefore, I could not have heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out what you meant when you said that you heard about it in some talks. What was the nature of these talks? If it wasn't at the collegium meeting, at which meeting did you hear talk about the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at meetings. I heard about it in contacts, but I didn't attach any importance to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever in that same period hear - and when I say that period, not just the conflict, the period, the months, preceding the conflict - hear for the Inter-Departmental Staff For Combatting Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of 1998 when we were resolving problems as to how best solutions could be found for the mobilisation of some units, because at that time we were carrying out reforms, I heard that a coordination body had been set up which was supposed to resolve problems related to both coordination between the army and other subjects in the implementation of defence tasks. I heard "coordinating body."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know who were members -- who were the members of this coordinating body?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was sufficient for me to know what the purpose of this coordinating body was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just have a comment to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you become chief of organization?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of department for organization, I think it was the 1st of September, 1994, when I became that, and at the same time, that means that that is the deputy head of the third administration, too. And on the 1st of April, 1999, I became the representative of that administration. So basically from 1994 onwards I dealt with organization at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, shouldn't the organization and membership of the coordinating body for fighting terrorism in Kosovo in 1998 come within your purview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was very specific at the very outset. I was in charge of organizing the army; that is to say, everything that has to do with military command of units and institutions was created and defined in my administration signed by the Chief of General Staff, and every such document is there to this day. The organization of these virtual organs and organs of the state were not within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're saying that the coordinating organ fighting terrorism in Kosovo is something you describe as a virtual organ? Just tell me briefly what do you mean when you say a "virtual organ"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All institutions of the system are clearly defined in the constitution and laws. In certain situations when institutions of the system cannot resolve in the best way a particular problem, then so-called temporary or virtual organs are set up to resolve a certain problem. People work on that in addition to their basic line of work. It is not their basic line of work. When that problem is resolved, then that particular organ is dissolved too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But a virtual organ coordinating body which involved or included among its membership senior members of the VJ, including corps commanders, would not come within your purview in the department of organization of the VJ? You would not know about how they were organized and their membership?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly cannot be within that domain, because all the members who were there had their regular activity and regular duties in their own organizational units where they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic -- oh, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, problems with the cables under the table. Mr. Stamp just opened new topic, so if you allow me just with two or three questions to clarify some things, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which topic are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: About command and about VJ system, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, it's me again. Just one more question. We've already heard about 1998 that you had confirmation from representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross. Am I right that in 1998 and 1999 the chains of command in the Army of Yugoslavia were fully preserved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right, and it is particularly my duty to say that institutions of command had been preserved and organized in a proper way and they functioned appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one question then arising from that, Mr. Kosovac. If you don't know about the coordinating bodies and what they are doing, how can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've made a sweeping statement about the chains of command in the Army of Yugoslavia being fully preserved throughout 1998 and 1999. Now, how can you know that beyond the things that you personally are doing when you do not know what the activities of the inter-departmental staff were or the Joint Command were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was very precise and I tried to be very precise. I said that the institutions of the system, the units of command that I was in charge of were organized in a proper way and that they functioned. A coordinating body, if it did exist, did not exist in the chain and institutions of the military, and I said that I either did or did not hear about that in 1999. After 1999 there has been a lot of talk about that but in different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything else, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour. Just, if you need clarification, General Kosovac mentioned KZB, which means operation in 2001 in relation to joint forces, Serbian forces, in border belt administration, border belt of Kosovo -- between Kosovo and Serbia, and that was a similar issue about the Joint Command, as I read in the newspapers and some other articles. So if you need clarification in that way, I could ask this witness about that issue some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not in this answer, though, that he's just given. You're not saying it's been misinterpreted, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think that the witness clarified some things, very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. And when he was asked about the Joint Command he said it was never discussed in any of the collegium meeting of the assistant Chief of Staff that he attended, but he had heard mention of it in passing but attached no importance to it. And that evidence referred to 1999. Is that correct? Or perhaps we should clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I heard the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, when you told us you had heard mention of "Joint Command," your answer was that you had heard mention of it during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: First question, General, pertains to what Mr. Ivetic was asking you about. He suggested to you that certain levels, or rather, higher levels of the MUP were not informed about the order on resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P1457. The lower part of the exhibit, please, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you just read who copies of this order were sent to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that the order should be sent to the Pristina Corps, the commander of the PJPs, the special units of the police in Kosovo and Metohija, and the Nis Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another subject now. In response to Mr. Ivetic's question on page 26 and 27 of today's transcript, this had to do with Article 17, or rather, your explanation of Article 17. You said that Article 17 precisely regulated a good solution; however, later on you said that the system of armed forces and the security forces was not properly organized and the security system, and that that is actually why there were certain problems. Can you tell us what it was that you meant when you said that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that answer I tried to be precise very briefly; namely, the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that came into being as a consequence of the transformation and orientation towards a completely different course. And on the basis of laws, systems were not clearly defined, like the security sector, like the armed forces, and the system of defence. When these sectors, or rather, when these concepts are clearly defined, then it is much clearer how to regulate mutual coordination, cooperation, relations, and everything else. That was poorly regulated and that is what was worked upon several times and proposals were submitted to state organs to have this regulated. As for Articles 16 and 17 that pertain to the actual implementation in the area of responsibility, it gives a great deal of clarity to the actual organs carrying this out, what they should do, and it says here, Familiarise them within their own areas of responsibility, where this is actually taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you said that several times -- I'm actually trying to find the reference. You said that several times the Army of Yugoslavia drew the attention of certain state organs to the fact that there was a certain discrepancy in the functioning of these systems and the army drew attention to that and gave certain proposals to state organs to that effect. Can you be more specific on that, what it was that the Army of Yugoslavia did in terms of these attempts to have these discrepancies in the system redressed -- or actually, why these discrepancies in the system actually did come into being. Let's start with the second part of my question. Why was there such a degree of discrepancy in the system?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give a very brief and effective answer. First of all, the discrepancy came into being because the systems were not defined. For 40 years there had been a socialist system, and then there was a transformation of the country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say I don't understand this question and therefore it's -- the answer is not helping me. Are you saying this arose in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is based on the witness's answer on page 27, the first four lines, when he said in response to Mr. Ivetic's questions on Article 17, he said that it's a system well regulated in accordance with Article 17; however, in order to have this function, or rather, the problem was that the system of armed forces and the security system was not properly regulated and that is why there were problems that came up. Now I'm trying to examine that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're quite right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's see where we broke off. Well, you know, General, don't you. I'm sure you do.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1996 what was felt was a discrepancy in the system and a lack of definition in the sector of defence, the security system, and General Kovacevic headed a Working Group and I was a member of this group. This Working Group was supposed to make proposals as to how to resolve the problem of command in the best possible way, in the sector of security and the system of defence and so on. This Working Group worked seven days in Fruska Gora and it prepared some material where it clearly defined what the supreme commander is what the Supreme Command is, what the staff of the Supreme Command is, what the rights and responsibilities were, and this proposal was submitted to proposal state authorities. The proposal was not carried through by way of changing the constitution and laws, but it was accepted as a good definition of the problems involved. The Chief of General Staff ordered in 1998 to set up a Working Group that was supposed to resolve the problem of coordinating and commanding between the army and the Ministry of the Interior. This Working Group worked in December and January, although we were expecting an aggression against the country to take place at any moment. This Working Group, this Working Group achieved good results, but they did not go into force because the war started. Many of these results were materialised later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is about Mr. Stamp's examination, page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D481, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, Mr. Stamp asked you this question on page 43, lines 10 and 11, Do you see paragraph 2 of item 2.1? I'm asking you the same question now. Do you see paragraph 2 of item 2.1?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So what's paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prohibit admission of members of paramilitary units, groups, and individuals already present in the area of responsibility to VJ commands and installations as volunteers without prior completion of procedures regulated by this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you looking at both the English and the Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And where is paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question in relation to that -- what about paragraph 2 of 2.1, was it written in order for persons to be admitted into the ranks of volunteers who were already paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written to prevent admission of paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I think there is something that is still not clear. May I get on with my question and you can see if I'm right or not, but check this page, page 49, line 22 -- 53, line 6--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought it was 49 --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 49, line 22, that's the first thing. If you could please have a look, the Chamber. There is the word "coordinating body," and then 53, line 6, and then the answer to your question there is a term that is used in both of these and the latter term -- I think it might be good to clarify what exactly the term implies in these cases, but the Chamber must grant permission for that or perhaps the Chamber could simply look into the use of this term. It's about terminology and it's about two different years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it's the Joint Command you're concerned about, is it the Joint Command you're concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness made it clear on two occasions that he heard about it during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that, but in 1998 he talks about a coordinating body; in 1999 again on page 53, line 6, he talks about a coordinating body that he heard of or did not hear of back in 1999. And you ask him about the Joint Command. So I don't know if the coordinating body and the Joint Command mean the same thing for him or is he using these two as two entirely different concepts to mean two different things. Is that the essence. Is it either or, or rather, is both the same thing? If you think that's worth looking into raising the issue, by all means do so, if you think I'm totally off the mark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you wish to ask a question of the witness to clarify this, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, General, you said that in 1998 you had heard of some coordinating body and then you said in 1999 maybe you heard and maybe you didn't hear of a coordinating body, if indeed, such a body if it existed at all. And then the Presiding Judge, His Honour, asked you, and you said that during the war in 1999 you heard about the Joint Command. What I want to know is: Are these two the same thing or are these two different things? Who did you hear this from, when, and what did it mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supposed to speak about 1999, and I meant to be very precise. In 1999 I heard those terms, coordinating body, Joint Command, both. I didn't go into the meaning or the respective meanings of these two. And, by the way, I think I pointed out that I had understood the meaning only in the year 2000 and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what was the meaning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious to anyone who deals with organisational matters that it seems that somebody called this coordinating body the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I press on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a matter for you, Mr. Fila. I do not require to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't require to know any more about this. The position's fairly clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think based -- since counsel has addressed or has commented in respect to the evidence, the witness spoke of a coordinating body when he was asked about the joint staff the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm clear on that, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Fila's problem is, but he should have a chance to clarify it if he feels there is an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This coordinating body that you've just mentioned, there was some coordinating body that was termed the Joint Command, that's in 1999, right? Can you explain now what you mean when you say that. What would be the job of this body?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a war being waged against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this required everybody's involvement, all those within the country. There was no unified system enabling all participants to organize themselves under a unified control or management and to all work toward the same goal. In order to prevent this a coordinating body was created in order to coordinate all the participants so that they all do their jobs with no interference or overlap. This is coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So is this subordination as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is coordination. When you have subordination, you get precise orders, you have responsibilities, you have reports, and I said that command units in the army were functioning and they were organized in a clear manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I hope this helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in case you're in any doubt, Mr. Fila, the answer -- one of the answers you were concerned about on page 49, line 22, was given specifically in relation to 1998. The witness said "1998" in spite of what he's now said about the purpose of him giving evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So was this coordinating body also in relation to 1998? Did you say anything about 1998?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in 1998 there was coordination as well. I'm not sure whether it was the same body doing it or not but I don't think it really makes any difference. There was coordination between all the participants, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does anything arise from that for you, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For you, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kosovac, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is General Zlatoje Terzic, number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, before we start your examination, can you just state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I am Zlatoje Terzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you talk to the Ojdanic Defence team and did you make a statement to us on the 18th of August, 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which you signed, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you go through this statement in preparation for this testimony? If asked the same questions before this Court, would you provide answers that are identical to what you said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I think there is a single exception in paragraph 5, there's a technical error; everything else I can corroborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, paragraph 5 of the B/C/S statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, General Terzic draws my attention to a technical error in paragraph 5 where it says 3D, he would like for those two letters, or rather, the number and the letter to be erased, because this is in reference to an exhibit that has not been admitted. So that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what has that got to do with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The General said that there was a small exception in paragraph 5, a technical error. I'm trying to specify what the error is in order to prevent us wasting anymore time, that's paragraph 5 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My problem here, Mr. Visnjic, is I haven't seen this statement. It may be my oversight in not looking at it, but this witness is, I think, still billed to be a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The statement was uploaded in B/C/S on the 12th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There does not appear to be a translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a glitch then, since we do have a translation and it's available in the re-list. 3D1093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the practice that we have which does not appear to be being followed by your case manager is to send both B/C/S and English versions of a statement as attachments to an e-mail. That does not appear to have happened in this case. We're about to have a break and we will take it early to try to resolve the problem and also to resolve the issue with the witness because it doesn't seem to me to be his responsibility to tell us what has and has not been admitted and what numbers should be assigned to exhibits. That's a matter for you to deal with. Mr. Terzic, we have a problem with your statement at the moment and that has to be resolved. We would have to have a break for 30 minutes in any event, so we'll take that break now. We'll resume at quarter to 1.00. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now see the problem, a meaningless 3D in paragraph 5, all right, but it wasn't easy for us to follow that without the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I hope that we have now resolved this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we'd like to tender this statement as Defence Exhibit 3D1093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit 3D712, it's an e-court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, early in 1998 the VJ started educating its staff in the international humanitarian law at the higher -- at the highest possible level of command and General Staff. Appearing in front of you in a minute should be a document dated the 3rd of February, 1998, this is an order for the execution of a seminar. Can you tell us more about this project, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: In February 1998 the then-deputy Chief of General Staff, Dragoljub Ojdanic, signed an order to organize a seminar in international humanitarian law of war for the leaders in the defence sector, the defence ministry, and the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this project involved a number of experts, did it not, international speakers. As far as I gathered by looking at the documents that paved the way for that seminar, the talks continued throughout 1998 or the preparations continued. If we turn back to page 2, you said that General Ojdanic signed this order. What exactly was his involvement in preparing this seminar after signing this order and then all the way until the seminar actually started?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I headed an administration at that time, and this administration was responsible for training and education of the entire Yugoslav Army. While preparing for this seminar, Ojdanic asked me on a number of occasions how the preparations were going. Several days before the seminar took place he wanted detailed information on the preparations. A mere day before the seminar started I went to see him and he went with me through all the documents about the preparation of this seminar. He called all the participants, phoned all the participants in my presence, told them about how important this seminar was and told them that attendance was compulsory. He also said that at the collegium meeting of the General Staff he underlined the importance of this seminar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D713.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have here a list of participants for this seminar, those from the General Staff of the VJ. Can you tell us briefly who was there on behalf of the Yugoslav side, who took part?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: You see the list, there are 26 names on it, 10 or 12 of these generals. These are chiefs or deputy chiefs in all the bodies that made up the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The beginning of the seminar was scheduled for the 25th of November, 1998, was it not. That morning, General - and we know this from other evidence - there was a replacement at the head of the General Staff and this was General Ojdanic's first day in this new post, despite which General Ojdanic turned up for the seminar, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit 3D711.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us about the substance of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: This is General Ojdanic's contribution. He introduces the seminar, he welcomes all of those present. Let me point out General Ojdanic was going to be there throughout for the whole seminar, but that morning he took up his duties as Chief of the General Staff. So he couldn't be there all the time, but in addition to welcoming those present he invited all the participants to have an open and well-argued discussion, including issues in relation to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender General Ojdanic's speech or contribution, it speaks for itself. I'm not going through it in any great detail with this witness; rather, I'll ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, how long did the seminar go on for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You say that General Ojdanic invited the participants to contribute to an open and reasoned discussion including Kosovo. Can you tell us what sort of discussion was there at the seminar?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: The seminar consisted of two parts, the first was contributions by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just a minute, please. As you go about answering this, can we please have 3D715 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: -- And representatives of the VJ. The discussion was open. There were differences of opinion, disagreements. For example, the high envoy of the International Committee of the Red Cross, an Australian, in his contribution pointed out that the national state at this point in history must renounce on some of its sovereignty in favour of the international community. Those who refused to do this would be excluded from the economic developments or would be forced renounce on some of their sovereignty by the use of arms. I was the person chairing this seminar at the moment when Mr. Sanderson spoke about this. I asked him to clarify what exactly he meant when he said the international community and in what way he was authorised to speak on behalf of the international community. He didn't answer the first of my questions and in answer to my second question he mentioned the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. This document in front of us is actually the report that you compiled at the end of the seminar. Who was this report submitted to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: This is the report - just a moment, please - that I submitted to the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Ojdanic, which is not customary because he was not my immediate superior because during the break after his remarks he ordered me to submit to him personally an extensive report on the seminar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is a document that contains several pages, and if I can put it that way it gives a concise version of all the statements at the seminar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Trial Chamber please see the English text on page 5, paragraph 3; B/C/S page 5, paragraph 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, so the methodology of this report is to give a brief version of all the statements made?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: It's a standard report. It contains what is important in a certain activity, like all reports that are compiled by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender the report in its entirety. Could the witness please be shown 3D714. The previous exhibit was 3D715, but now I would like 3D714.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have yet another report in front of us on the same subject also sent to the Chief of General Staff. This time it was signed by Major-General Professor Dr. Sinisa Borovic. What was the position of General Borovic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: He was assistant Chief of General Staff and at the same time he was head of the sector and my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower and into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So he submitted this report to General Ojdanic down the regular chain?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic, had he not ordered me to give my report to him in person, I would have sent it to General Borovic and he would have submitted it to General Ojdanic. In this situation, of course, I submitted a copy to him, as well, but he found it necessary to inform General Ojdanic briefly about this activity that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone and slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you slow down a little bit, please, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Terzic, this document suggests that it was the position of all the representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross that the modern world requires that some sovereignty has to be conceded to international bodies. You confined the reference earlier to Mr. Sanderson. Does this refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was only Mr. Sanderson that had such a position, no one else. Here for the sake of summarizing it is possible to understand things that way; however, in my report it is stated unequivocally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D715 that is actually the report of General Terzic has a total of nine pages. Due to its volume, I did not want to go through it in detail, but you will find references to each and every participant in terms of what he said, of course again in a summarized form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us go back now to this exhibit, 3D714, and the last paragraph of this exhibit at that. There is an interesting statement here that the representatives of the ICRC asked for the lecture of Dr. Djordje Radojevic on the training of the law of war in the Army of Yugoslavia to be authorised and published in the ICRC bulletin in Geneva in 1999. General, can you tell us a bit more about this, what it was that Colonel Radojevic spoke about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Dr. Djordje Radojevic was involved in the seminar. At the seminar he spoke about the content of international humanitarian law in the curriculum and training of all structures of the Army of Yugoslavia. It was very well received, his statement was, and the representatives of the ICRC asked him to submit a copy of his remarks so they could publish it in the ICRC bulletin at the same time as an example to others as to how this subject matter should be approached in training and educating the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you have any more precise information about this? Let us just represent this for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to tire anyone, so very briefly where NCOs are trained there are four periods devoted to regulations in this field and at the military academy there is eight classes per week. At the command staff academy there is 16 classes in terms of command, that subject, and at the highest school of national defence there are six classes devoted to the subject of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of practical training, this subject matter was given particular attention. For example, what was particularly appreciated were protected facilities, facilities that could cause a catastrophe if they were to be destroyed it could cause a catastrophe, like chemical facilities, dams, and so on, then also how to treat civilians, prisoners of war, and so on. Also what was being taught was that every command is duty-bound in its report to report about all violations of norms of international humanitarian law and laws of war, both those committed by their own members and by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, just one thing in terms of the interpretation. Your answer was that at the highest level, that is to say the national defence school, there are six classes devoted to international humanitarian law that are part of the subject, what subject?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Warfare is the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Warfare. Thank you. General, the seminar was over, as we said, towards the end of November. Is that where education stopped, this seminar?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't even start with this seminar. Up until this seminar, several were held, seven I think, and this was the eighth one that was carried out by the ICRC for the highest levels of command in the Army of Yugoslavia and one seminar was held for instructors; that is to say, officers, members of the army, who after that held seminars in various units. What was envisaged was to continue these seminars in cooperation with the ICRC. All of this on the basis of an agreement between the minister of defence and the ICRC. If I am not mistaken, it was signed in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal asserts there was a plan for expelling Albanians and that this plan was made by the -- by October 1998 at the latest. You've already responded to that in paragraph 22 of your statement. Now I would like to ask you, in view of this assertion made by the OTP, to comment on it in view of the activities taken by General Ojdanic and the General Staff towards the end of 1998 in 1999 as well, both in the field of training and in the field of seminars devoted to international humanitarian law and ultimately in terms of training volunteers, which is what you testified to in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, these activities and such an assertion are incompatible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had seen some exhibits noted by the Lukic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, they have shaken their head --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Already, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. I want to ask you, when did you --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you retire or when did you leave the VJ, what year?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I was retired in 2003 on the 1st of June officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did that come about, could you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: By way of a decision of the president, or rather, the minister of defence at the time, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did that have anything to do in connection with your work with the VJ Commission on Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I could not answer that for you. With Mr. Tadic who was then minister of defence, I talked to him for two hours and he did not object to anything in relation to the work of that commission and my work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, didn't Mr. Tadic dissolve that commission on the 11th of April, 2003?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Well, the minister of defence and the Chief of General Staff established the commission; it was their right to decide whether they would dissolve it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the minister of defence and the chairman or the Chief of the General Staff who created the commission were, in fact, different individuals, right? That was Slobodan Krapovic as the minister of defence in 2001 and General Pavkovic as the Chief of General Staff in 2001 when that commission was created, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the ostensible purpose of that commission when it was created?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I think that I can speak about this subject matter although I have not received a waiver with regard to these topics, because the document on the establishment of the commission was a public one. The commission was established by the minister of defence and the Chief of General Staff, with the agreement of the federal government. As an advisory body, I underline, an advisory body of the minister of defence and the Chief of General Staff in relation to cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was some controversy in Serbia between 2001 and 2003 about the activities and the role of this commission; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to what the tabloids wrote, then yes; otherwise, I do not know about any other controversy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And which -- which newspapers or which media are you referring to when you use the term "tabloids," could you name them for us, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part several of them. Now, for me to give you the names -- well, to tell you the truth I wasn't even following all of that. I know it was published by Blic, Kurir. I wouldn't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: B92 radio?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I don't listen to that. I didn't listen to them at the time, I didn't hear them say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Beta, are you familiar with Beta?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Beta, yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: But I don't know about Beta reporting about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you refer to Beta as a tabloid?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Exhibit P2935 we have a couple of articles, one of them is from Beta dated the 15th of April, 2003, which is reporting that you, General Terzic, were dismissed by the defence minister and that you had been the head of the Commission For Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Is that correct, you were head of commission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I was head of the commission. I was president of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us who the other members of the commission were, were they all members or retired members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: At that time, only one was a retired member of the Army of Yugoslavia, that was General Gojovic, all the others were from different structures of the General Staff and the ministry, these were people who were still employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Geza Farkas was one of the members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Geza Farkas I think was retired after that, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But he was one of the members?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Sreten Obrencevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Sreten Obrencevic later became a member of the commission, he wasn't a member from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Milos Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: He also became a member later, only in the following year, 2002, whereas the commission was established in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, you said that you were retired on the 1st of June, and this report is suggesting that you had been dismissed from the VJ commission by the 15th of April. When was the decision made that you should be retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My service stopped on the 1st of June. There is a procedure involved, and that is what I meant when I said the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, was Radomir Gojovic also a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Milan Gvero?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're saying he was never a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: He was never a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about two more, Dusan Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Never, never, he was never a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about a non-paid member?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last one is General Bosko Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: He was never a member of the commission either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are there other members that I haven't named?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Colonel Mojsilovic was secretary of the commission. There were a few other members as well, but I'm not sure that I'm going to recall all of the names. After all, all of that is contained in the documentation and the orders and it's not a problem to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. And the controversy I referred to and which you said apparently is only as a result of what the tabloids were publishing, that controversy suggested that the commission was known as the anti-Hague lobby. Did you ever hear that term used in connection with your commission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I heard all sorts of expressions, but I would kindly ask you to have a look at my reports to the minister of defence and the Chief of General Staff, and from them you will be able to conclude for yourself that this commission was in no way an anti-Hague lobby.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was one of your reports to the commission in connection with the existence of VJ files for General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're not familiar with an OTP request for certain of those files and you being involved and denying that such files existed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, since I received several hundred requests at the time, the commission did, that is, in that period of time, it is very hard for me now to give yes or no answers in relation to individual requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we're not talking about some private or sergeant, we're talking about General Mladic who's one of the two most-wanted fugitives of this Tribunal. You know who he is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't recall that there was an OTP request and that you personally were indicating that there were no such files in existence, VJ files for General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: The commission did not formulate answers on its own. Once a request was received from the OTP -- well, since the commission did not have any original documents, when OTP requests were received, first through the Ministry of Defence and later on through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the commission would write letters to individual addresses with questions related to the documents sought. The answers we got from them later became answers of the commission. The commission did not formulate any answer on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, with regard to whether or not there were any VJ files in existence for General Mladic, wouldn't you in the VJ be in a better position to know about that than the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: We are not understanding each other. I didn't ask the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to submit this information to me. It is through them that I received OTP requests. As for these requests in terms of whether there are any dossiers on General Mladic, I sent that to the personnel administration of the Ministry of Defence or General Staff and the security administration; so what I got from them was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the security administration, you mean the security administration of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Personnel administration of the General Staff that is in charge of personal files.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if you passed on information back in response to the OTP request that there were no files in existence for General Mladic, that's because that was the information you had received from the personnel and security administrations of the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, because I could not know whether something like that did or did not exist or did I have any files or dossiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a question about that. Exhibit 2935, the second story in that exhibit is a report from Radio B92 and it claims that the commission possessed somewhere around 14.000 documents. Your commission did have a lot of documents, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: The commission did not have a single document whatsoever. This assertion is based on the following. The commission in this period of its work submitted to the OTP 14.000 pages of requested documents, 14.000 pages of requested documents, pages requested by you. How and why somebody provided this kind of information that we had 14.000 pages of documents, I really don't know. I repeat, the commission never had original documents or could it take them or do anything with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what exactly did you and all these other generals do then on this Commission For Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: I have to clarify, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Whenever we received a request from the OTP or from one of the Defence teams for that matter, because the commission did not have any documents we would -- we would write to all the tactical leaders in the Army of Yugoslavia for them to inform us whether such documents existed to begin with, and secondly to inform us about their position as to whether these documents could be forwarded or not. Once we received feedback from them, if the feedback was positive, affirmative to both questions, then there was no further procedure to follow. If the reply was that the document existed but they believed that because of state security it should not be forwarded to the OTP, then the members of the mission would get together with whoever was in possession of this document to review the issue. And normally we would try to convince them because it was the position of our commission that each and every document should be forwarded to the OTP. We underlined this fact in all of our reports, and every time I briefed my superiors I spoke about that. I tried to get them to -- we tried to get them to change their position in a bid to get the document forwarded to the OTP. Just to back this up, the National Council for Cooperation with the Tribunal accepted all of the commission's decisions. There was a single decision at a later stage that was amended, but a reasoned explanation was provided. I'm sorry if I said "decisions," I meant proposals. We made no decisions, we made proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned requests from Defence teams, and you're aware, aren't you, sir, from the Milosevic trial that there was some controversy regarding the commission because there was a suspicion on the part of the OTP and a suggestion that your commission was providing documents to Mr. Milosevic which were not forthcoming to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I must say this again, the commission never had a single original document. The originals were kept by the -- those who were in charge of this in the archives. As chairman of the commission, I did not have the right to order that any document be photocopied. The only person who had this power was Chief of the General Staff. Therefore, I was in no position to provide anyone with documents, aside from the procedure that I have now familiarised you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My understanding of the commission then is although you may not have had in your possession original documents, you'd had the ability to control whether or not those documents would be released to the OTP or Mr. Milosevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: No. The commission did not forward documents to the OTP or the Defence. It only forwarded documents to the defence ministry, and they then decided what to do with it. And then later the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or the National Council, in both cases we would submit our report containing all of our positions, and this was forwarded to the defence minister. The commission never forwarded documents directly to the OTP or to any of the defence teams. This was the only procedure that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But your commission was the first stop in deciding whether or not documents might eventually be forwarded to the OTP or General Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic, Slobodan Milosevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Again, not correct. What we did was make proposals to the defence minister and then to the chairman of the National Council for Cooperation with the Tribunal. We made proposals on what to do and the decision was made first by the defence minister and then by the chairman of the National Council. They could either accept or overrule our proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From what you said earlier, I take it that there was only one time where the proposal of the commission was disagreed with; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. First it was adopted, and then it was amended a month later; however, an explanation was provided and I can provide more detail about this, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess my question about that is: What was your initial proposal in connection with that document? Was your initial proposal that it be released or that it not be released?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't about a document this time, because the commission, apart from working with the Tribunal on the issue of documents, it also dealt with missing persons, not in terms of actually finding missing persons but to keep things running as they were supposed to be running. There was a request that was made for a waiver in terms of keeping a state secret in relation to someone who had already violated these norms governing state secrets. I personally and other members of the commission believed that it wasn't all right to grant somebody a waiver after the fact, and thus to release them from their responsibility. So that was the only difference. The Supreme National Council accepted our position. A month later; however, and they had their own reasons I won't go into that, they amended their position and they approved this waiver; however, they did provide a reasoned explanation in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for a minute, Your Honour, I would like to ask the name of this individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, I'd like to ask one thing. Mr. Terzic, I don't understand at the moment the purpose of this body the way you've explained it. You already had a Commission For Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and no doubt they sent requests to the Ministry of Defence when they received them; is that correct? Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at first, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why couldn't a clerk in the Ministry of Defence process these to the responsible departments? Why was it necessary to have a high-powered commission of senior personnel from the Ministry of Defence, the VJ, and retired generals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Law on the Establishment of the National Council envisages two commissions. One of these is defence and internal affairs, so that's the law. What you said, for a simple clerk to be forwarding documents such as these, you must understand that a simple clerk would not be able to assess the importance of certain documents and then go back to the tactical mainstay and say regardless of your position that this document should not be sent, I think it should still be sent. It just wouldn't work that way, would it? As to the reasons why the commission was set up, I don't think I'm best-placed necessarily to answer this question. I think Krapovic and other people should talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm left wondering whether it didn't work the other way, that you were a filter to prevent documents getting to The Hague Tribunal, because you had the expertise to assess the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 88 per cent of the requests made by the Tribunal were carried out. Only those that were impossible to carry out were not carried out. For example, it was requested that documents be sent from battalion to General Staff level, all of their documents within a seven-month deadline [as interpreted] and 20 days' deadline, and these are truck-loads of documents. I'm not going into their relevance, but it was a technical impossibility to comply with that deadline and with the request. Documents were requested from all military courts over a ten-year period, all the documents, every single document over a ten-year period. I addressed Carla del Ponte three times on this issue when she came to Belgrade. I told her that these requests should be stream-lined so that we were able to deal with them again. Every time I briefed anyone, anyone written report that I sent to anyone, and I suppose the OTP are in possession of those, I don't know, I hadn't prepared for this subject matter to be raised. This had not been announced, but I always advocated the need to submit all the documents to the OTP, firstly so that we may wash ourselves clean of the accusation of not being cooperative; and secondly, I personally knew that there was absolutely nothing in those documents that should keep us from handing these over to the Tribunal. I said this, I wrote this on a number of occasions, and I signed these positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll go into private session briefly for the purpose indicated by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one translation issue in the transcript page 86, line 6, seven-month time-period was what was said, not deadline. I just want to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, in your answer just before we went into private session when speaking to Judge Bonomy you said: "I personally knew there was absolutely nothing in those documents ..." You're talking about all the documents that were being requested by the OTP? You didn't personally review all those documents yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: Based on all my information, my contact with tactical mainstays -- just let me make sure we understand each other. There was nothing that accused the state, nothing material. At the same time, there was nothing material that was of any consequence or that might prove prejudicial to state security. So those are the two elements I'm talking about. I'm not saying -- not necessarily saying there was not something contentious in a given document, from your point of view, when I say contentious, I mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you're not a lawyer, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I guess I'm curious as to how you would know who would be material in terms of evidential value for the Prosecution in a case like this or the other cases that are being prosecuted in The Hague Tribunal, not only against Serbs, but also against Muslims, Croatians, Albanians, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC
utterances.text: That's what I said. I wasn't talking about your point of view. I'm talking about the national security point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a bit more to go. I wonder if we can break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we have any option. It's an unfortunate feature of this place, Mr. Terzic, that we have to stick rigidly to our time allocation because another case comes into this room in the afternoon. So we have to break at this stage and continue tomorrow, that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. You should be here, ready to resume your evidence at that stage. Meanwhile, it is vital that you should have no discussion with anyone at all about the evidence in the case; that doesn't stop you meeting with and talking to people, but there must be absolutely no discussion of the evidence. And the best way to do that, of course, is to stay away from the people involved in the case. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24
